references.text: The context of the healing: Jesus met ten lepers and sent them to the priests, and they were cleansed on the way ([ref:Luk 17:12-14|Luke 17:12-14]). Verse 17 refers back to these ten who were cleansed.
Only one of the ten – a Samaritan – returned to thank Jesus ([ref:Luk 17:15-16|Luke 17:15-16]). Jesus' question in verse 17 highlights the contrast between the one grateful and the nine ungrateful.

Naaman was cleansed of his leprosy by dipping himself seven times in the Jordan ([ref:2 Kong 5:14|2 Kings 5:14]). He was a foreigner who was cleansed and returned in gratitude – a parallel to the Samaritan man, who was the only one of ten to return.

The Mosaic law prescribed that the leper should show himself to the priest to be declared clean ([ref:3 Mos 14:2-3|Leviticus 14:2-3]). Jesus sent the ten to the priests in accordance with this, and the expression "was cleansed" (ἐκαθαρίσθησαν) in verse 17 relates to this cleansing ritual.

The psalmist exhorts himself: "My soul, bless the Lord, and forget not all his benefits!" ([ref:Sal 103:1-2|Psalm 103:1-2]). Jesus' question "Where are the nine?" is an implicit accusation of ingratitude – they forgot to return and praise God for his benefit.

Isaiah laments over Israel's ingratitude: "Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me" ([ref:Jes 1:2-3|Isaiah 1:2-3]). The nine lepers who did not return illustrate a similar pattern of receiving God's grace without gratitude.

Paul describes people as "knowing God, yet neither glorifying him nor giving thanks to him" ([ref:Rom 1:21|Romans 1:21]). The nine cleansed who did not return to give God glory illustrate precisely this lack of gratitude toward God.
